name: Brazil 2002 (Scolari)
scopeNote: Brazil at the 2002 World Cup (Korea/Japan) under Luiz Felipe Scolari: first match Brazil 2-1 Turkey, Ulsan, 3 June 2002; final Brazil 2-0 Germany, Yokohama, 30 June 2002 (seven wins out of seven). Qualifying (troubled 2000-01 campaign under Leao and Luxemburgo; Scolari took over in June 2001 and lost his Montevideo debut to Uruguay) is EXCLUDED and no earlier manager is included; the friendlies and Copa America 2001 build-up only appear as context. Sources name the shape 3-5-2 (AP, Fox, SI, TFT), 3-4-2-1 (Holding Midfield) or 3-4-1-2 (blogs); the 'Familia Scolari' label came from the media (Tosta/Folha, per Scolari himself), not from Scolari. Blogs claiming 3-4-3 or a 'fluid 3-2-5' are tier D and ignored. No tier A tactical study (FIFA TSG, Coaches' Voice tactical piece, Zonal Marking) was reachable, so pressing, marking and set pieces are thin.
openQuestions: Midfield: Holding Midfield says Juninho + Emerson behind the 3Rs in a 3-4-2-1 and that Gilberto Silva replaced the injured Emerson; The42/FourFourTwo describe 'two deep-lying midfielders' (Gilberto Silva + Kleberson). Both are true at different moments (Juninho started the early games; Kleberson replaced Juninho from the Belgium game onward). Confirm the exact starting XI per match.

Zonal vs man marking: no source in this run says which. Denilson says only Ronaldo had no marking duty and the team pressed the German build-up, and Roque Junior is quoted on tall defenders handling long balls; neither names a marking system. Needs a tier A/B study (FIFA TSG 2002 report, Spielverlagerung, Jonathan Wilson).

Shape source: efdeportes (Oct 2002, Ole 17 July 2002) says Scolari said afterwards the system was a copy of Bielsa's Argentina; Scolari's own later interviews credit Geninho (Athletico-PR) for convincing him of three centre-backs. Contested credit.
Set pieces: only Ronaldinho's free-kick vs England and Roberto Carlos's goal vs Costa Rica are in evidence; no study of Brazil's set-piece organisation.

Pressing height: Holding Midfield says the defence sat deep and countered; Denilson says Brazil pressed the German build-up for the first goal. Likely a mid/low block with selective pressing, not confirmed.

sources.title: Scolari's Brazil (Holding Midfield)
sources.evidence: Set up in a 3-4-2-1, that trio made up the highest positioned players, whereas Juninho Paulista, himself an attacking midfielder, sat behind them with Emerson, acting as the link between the defence and attack while Emerson did the dirty work, along with wing-backs Roberto Carlos and Cafu. In front of the fairly average Marcos in goal was Lucio, Roque Junior and Edmilson – the latter having the license to bring the ball forward.

sources.title: Scolari's Brazil (Holding Midfield)
sources.evidence: The defence sat deep, relying more on numbers than great organisation to stop the opposition, which allowed plenty of space on the counter for that forward trio to manipulate.

sources.title: Scolari's Brazil (Holding Midfield)

sources.evidence: Emerson was injured days before the tournament began so Cafu was given the captain’s armband and Gilberto Silva, who was a surprise inclusion in the squad after a great season in which he had been moved from central defence into midfield, took his midfield spot.

sources.title: Deciphering Luiz Felipe Scolari (These Football Times)
sources.evidence: In Korea and Japan, at the 2002 World Cup, Scolari shifted from his traditional formation to a 3-5-2 and bet all his chips on Rivaldo and Ronaldo – both available after lengthy injuries – and bright young star, Ronaldinho.

sources.title: Deciphering Luiz Felipe Scolari (These Football Times)
sources.evidence: They complimented a quite brilliant defence, with Lúcio, Edmílson, and Roque Júnior the centre-backs, and Cafu and Roberto Carlos patrollign the flanks.

sources.title: Deciphering Luiz Felipe Scolari (These Football Times)
sources.evidence: With various other stars like Djalminha, Márcio Amoroso and Giovane Élber omitted from the squad, it was a gamble that paid immense dividends.

sources.title: Deciphering Luiz Felipe Scolari (These Football Times)
sources.evidence: The class of 2002 became known as the Família Scolari, consolidating the idea that the coach was a father figure to his “family” of players, creating an environment of loyalty and companionship fondly remembered by his star turns to this day.

sources.title: Deciphering Luiz Felipe Scolari (These Football Times)
sources.evidence: With the press, and many Brazilian fans, urging the manager to select the great Romário, Felipão trusted his instinct, leaving the 1994 champion at home, much to the chagrin of the media. He took the punches, threw some back, and headed to the Far East with supreme confidence.

sources.title: Deciphering Luiz Felipe Scolari (These Football Times)
sources.evidence: The trio scored 15 of the Seleção’s 18 goals in the tournament.

sources.title: Defensive strength Brazil's trump card as World Cup looms (FourFourTwo, Michael Cox)
sources.evidence: Brazil used three centre-backs in tandem with two holding midfielders, none of whom were technically remarkable footballers. Although Brazil's formation regularly changes, that's the usual theme - a solid backbone to the side gives the attackers freedom to roam.

sources.title: Defensive strength Brazil's trump card as World Cup looms (FourFourTwo, Michael Cox)
sources.evidence: the defensive base of his Brazil side is much more impressive than when he won this competition in 2002 - back then, he was forced to depend upon Roque Junior as one of his centre-backs.

sources.title: Brazil could go back to formation from 2002 title (AP/SI)
sources.evidence: Scolari used a 3-5-2 system when it claimed its fifth World Cup title in 2002, with the fullbacks allowed to attack more often.

sources.title: Brazil could go back to formation from 2002 title (AP/SI)

sources.evidence: Eight years later, Scolari played three central defenders and screened them with two unfashionable and dogged deep-lying midfielders. The front three and the wing-backs were granted freedom to create but the important thing was balance and Scolari got it just right.
